messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 77
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: School Principal
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 70

He was seventy-two when it happened, three years after retiring as a high school principal. The retirement had been a quiet ceremony—students crying, teachers hugging him—and after forty years of service he had looked forward to rest. He stayed active, volunteering at the school’s reading program twice a week. That afternoon he had stayed late to help a young teacher organize the library. The school was empty. He heard the side door rattle, and when he went to check, two young men pushed him into the storage room. They wanted money. He had only a few dollars in his wallet. They beat him with a metal pipe. He remembers the sound of his own ribs cracking, the taste of blood, the way his glasses shattered on the concrete. They left him on the floor, and it took half an hour before a janitor found him.

In the hospital he told the police he couldn’t identify the men. He couldn’t. The faces are still a blur. What he sees, instead, is the pipe—the way it swung, the arc of it, the light reflecting off the metal as it came down. That image comes to him now, suddenly, without warning. He will be standing at the front of the church on Sunday or sitting at the dinner table with his wife and the pipe appears in his mind, and he flinches. He drops his fork. His wife touches his arm and asks if he is all right. He says yes, but his heart is pounding, his palms are wet. He cannot concentrate on the sermon or the meal.

He thought he could manage. He returned to the school after six weeks, but he could not walk past the storage room. He started taking different routes through the hallways. Then he stopped volunteering altogether. He told the principal that his age made it difficult. In truth, he could not be inside the building without scanning every door, every corner. He began to stay home. His wife insisted on grocery shopping now; she does all the errands. He tells himself it is because the winter ice is dangerous for a man his age. But he knows.

At night he cannot sleep. He lies awake listening for the side door. He has installed three deadbolts on the front door of his house. He checks them before bed, then again at two in the morning, then again at four. His wife says he is wearing out the locks. He knows he is being unreasonable, but he cannot stop. The sound of a door closing anywhere—even in a television show—makes him gasp. He cannot watch movies with violence. He avoids news reports about crime. He has stopped reading the newspaper. His adult children call from overseas; he speaks to them for a few minutes, then says he is tired and hangs up. He used to be the one who told stories at family gatherings. Now he has nothing to say. He feels hollow, like the man who was beaten is not him anymore.

Three years later, his wife convinced him to come to my office. He sits very still in the chair, hands on his knees. He does not look around the room. He speaks quietly, precisely, the way a former principal might. He tells me he knows he is not the same. He says he used to be strong. Then his voice breaks, just slightly, and he says the worst part is not the pain he felt—it is that he cannot protect the people he loves. He cannot even protect himself. He hears a car door shut outside and his head snaps toward the window before he can stop it. He apologizes. He does not know how to go back to who he was.
